title: Automating hiring inbox without losing the relationship
metaTitle: A hiring inbox that still answers people
excerpt: Acknowledge applications and flag incomplete ones against criteria you wrote. A person still makes the rejection and the invitation to talk.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug. A hiring inbox can sort the pile; the decision should not leave an empty chair.
caption: The work is on the desk. A person still answers. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Can hiring software reject applicants on its own?
faqs.answer: It should not. It can mark an application incomplete when a required link is missing, and it can send a receipt that promises a real review date. A rejection, an interview, and any sentence about why someone was not chosen stay with a person who read the work.

faqs.question: What belongs in the criteria before you automate the inbox?
faqs.answer: Sentences you would say to a candidate: the craft, the kind of work in the portfolio, and practical facts such as a link that opens. Leave out prestige, gaps, and resemblance to the last hire. If you would not defend it, it is not a criterion.

faqs.question: Is a score useful for sorting applications?
faqs.answer: A single score will be treated as a decision by anyone in a hurry. Sort by checks you can name, such as whether the required link is present, and let a person order the rest. Hide the score if a tool insists on showing one.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Hiring inbox automation should acknowledge an application, check it against criteria you wrote down, and draft a first sort. A person makes the yes, the no, and anything in between. The candidate will remember the note you send longer than you will remember the minute you saved.

Automate the handoff around the first read. The machine may confirm receipt, file the materials, and mark gaps against a list. Keep a person on anything the candidate will see beyond that receipt, anything that sounds like an offer or a rejection reason you cannot stand behind, and anything you cannot undo, such as a public no or a calendar full of interviews you did not mean to book. Measure minutes of sorting against minutes of review, and count the replies you had to correct.

## Write the criteria before the inbox fills

A first read is only fair if the criteria exist as sentences, not as a vibe in the founder's head. Write them where the reviewer and the workflow can both see them. For a studio role, that might be a specific craft, a kind of work in the portfolio, and the practical facts you are allowed to require, such as a link that opens. For a client hiring with your help, the criteria are theirs, in their words, agreed before anyone applies.

Leave out anything you would not say to a candidate. If you would not defend it, it does not belong in the sort. A model will happily score on prestige, on a gap in a résumé, or on a writing style that resembles the last hire. Those are not criteria. They are shortcuts, and they are how a strong applicant gets a draft rejection that a person then has to unsay.

Separate "incomplete" from "no." Incomplete means a required link is missing or the file will not open. No means you read the materials and they do not meet a criterion you can name. Maybe means a person should look before any template runs. The workflow may label incomplete when a field is empty. It may not label no.

## What arrives, and what the machine may do

An application is a name, a contact, and a set of files or links. The old chore is the pile: downloading, checking that the link works, noticing a duplicate, and writing the same acknowledgement. Automate that pile.

1. Store the application with the role and the time.
2. Mark a duplicate if the same person applied twice, so they get one thread, not two tones.
3. Mark incomplete against the required fields only, in plain language: "portfolio link missing."
4. Draft an acknowledgement that says you received it and when a person will actually look.

The acknowledgement can send on its own only if the text is fixed, true, and free of judgment. "We have your application for the designer role. A person will review it by Friday" is a receipt, if Friday is real. "We were impressed by your background" is a judgment, and it waits, because you have not looked. Do not promise a Friday you cannot keep in order to sound responsive. Change the sentence when the week is heavy.

Do not auto-book interviews. Offering times is a decision that the person passed the first read. A link that lets every applicant hold the founder's calendar will fill the week with conversations you meant to have with three people. The draft may include a line a reviewer can add later, when they have said yes to a conversation.

Do not rank the pile with a single score. If you want an order, sort by the criteria you can check without taste first, such as "required link present," and let a person order the rest. A score of 74 will be treated as a decision by anyone in a hurry. Hide it.

## The note a person still sends

Rejections, interview offers, and "we are keeping your materials" are notes the candidate sees. A person sends them. The template can be kind and short. It should not invent a specific reason the model inferred. A false specific reason is worse than a general one, because the candidate can often tell it does not match their work, and you cannot defend it.

A general rejection that a person approved as policy is enough for the clear cases after a real read: you read the portfolio, it does not match the criterion, you send the template. The read is the part you cannot skip. A template on an unread application is a no you did not earn.

Offers of a conversation should say who the conversation is with, how long it is, and what you want to look at. They should not say the role is theirs. An interview is not an offer of work, and a sloppy draft will blur that. Compensation talk, if it belongs anywhere this early, belongs with a person who knows the range, not in a paragraph generated to sound welcoming.

If you need a second opinion on how a small team should set this up without pretending to be a large recruiting desk, book an [intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the role and the criteria, not a stack of résumés. The useful outcome is a first-read handoff you can explain to a candidate if they ask.

People read short notes quickly and long ones poorly. Nielsen Norman Group's [How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) describes the same pressure on the web: users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text on a page they do open. A candidate will read the first lines of your reply with care and skim the rest. Put the decision and the next step in those lines. Put the warmth in being accurate, not in a long preamble about your culture.

## What you never let the tool decide

Do not auto-reject. Not on a score, not on a keyword, not on a school, not on a gap. The incomplete label can ask for the missing link. A rejection is a person.

Do not let the tool write a "personalized" paragraph that praises a project it half-read. Candidates can see when the sentence does not match the work. A wrong compliment does more damage than a plain template. If you want one specific line, a person writes it after opening the portfolio, or you do not include one.

Do not forward the application to a client or a colleague with a generated verdict attached. Sharing a candidate's materials is a disclosure. A person chooses the audience. The verdict, if you share one internally, is labeled as a person's note, not as the system's conclusion.

Do not ask unlawful or irrelevant questions in the form so the model has more to score. Collect what you need to do the first read. Extra fields become extra ways to be unfair, and they sit in your records.

The acknowledgement's promise about timing is a promise. If you miss it, a person sends the update. An automated "we need more time" that fires forever is how candidates learn you do not mean the dates. Update the date in the template when the team is underwater. That is a smaller, better automation than a fiction.

## Minutes saved against minutes of review

Time a week of the old inbox. Include downloading files, checking links, writing acknowledgements, and the dread of a pile with no criteria. The criteria work is part of the project, not a tax on the tool. Without it there is nothing safe to automate.

Time the new review. Open the materials that the workflow marked ready, check the criterion you said mattered, and send the template or book the conversation yourself. If you are re-reading every incomplete application because the tool cries wolf, tighten the required fields. If you are scared to send the rejection template, you have not agreed the criteria. Fix that before you speed up.

Count corrections: candidates who reply that they already applied, that you praised the wrong project, or that you rejected them before the date you promised a review. Any of those means the receipt or the draft is overreaching. Pull it back to a shorter sentence.

Keep a person on every rejection and every interview offer, including after the system feels dull. The receipt can stay automatic when it has been true for a month. Dull and true is the goal. Fast and wrong is a story the candidate tells other people.

## A pile you can still look at

Once a week, a person looks at a sample of applications the workflow marked incomplete or duplicate, to see whether good people are stuck on a broken form. A form that rejects a portfolio hosted on an unusual domain is your bug, not their failure. Fix the check, and write to anyone you stalled if the stall was your fault.

Close the role in the workflow when the role is closed. Applications that arrive after that get a receipt that says the role is closed, which a person approved as a sentence. They do not get a rejection that pretends you compared them to the shortlist.

Keep the criteria next to the role, and change them in public inside the team when the role changes. A workflow running on last quarter's criteria will produce a confident sort that nobody believes, and then everyone returns to the unstructured pile you were trying to leave.

Stock is a different kind of queue, and the person who must not be surprised is sometimes the customer. [Automating inventory alerts without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-inventory-alerts-without-losing-the-relationship) is next, because a low-stock warning is useful inside the studio and dangerous when it becomes a promise the buyer can see.
